陶笛屬氣鳴壺笛，發聲靠氣流經哨口撞擊唇片，腔體以亥姆霍茲共振產生音高。其音色因共: The ocarina is an aerophone vessel flute; it sounds when air passes the voicing and strikes the lip, and the cavity produces pitch by Helmholtz resonance. Because the resonator selectively amplifies the fundamental, its timbre has few overtones, unlike the transverse flute and recorder, which sound by the length of a tube. Volume control is limited: the force of the breath mainly changes pitch rather than volume, by some semitones, so intonation is hard to keep. Range depends on the total area of the holes and the volume of the cavity; a common alto in C can play a twelfth from A to F, and multi-chamber instruments extend the range or sound several notes at once. Most vessel ocarinas do not overblow easily to overtones.

Its types can be traced to Chinese and Mesoamerican cultures; European courts received it through expeditions and it later became a toy. In nineteenth-century Italy Giuseppe Donati improved it into a ten-hole ocarina and gave it the name ocarina; in the twentieth century it spread to the United States and Asia, where Aketagawa Takashi in Japan added semitone holes to make the twelve-hole pattern, and John Taylor in England developed the four-hole English fingering system.

The ocarina is an aerophone of the vessel-flute class, H-S number 421.221.422. A typical instrument is a closed cavity with four to twelve fingerholes and a protruding mouthpiece; it is traditionally made of clay or ceramic, and also of plastic, wood, glass, metal or bone. The player blows through the mouthpiece, the air strikes the voicing, and the cavity resonates; covering the holes changes pitch, and the force of the breath also affects intonation. Similar instruments are found in Chinese song-and-dance and in Mesoamerican ritual, and it later reached European courts and the countryside, and is used today in orchestras, choirs and games.
